'''Anne Kernan''' (15 January 1933 – 11 May 2020) was an Irish [[Particle physics|particle physicist]].

==Early life and education==
Kernan was born in 1933 to Annie Connor and Frederick Kernan in [[Glasnevin]]. She was the second of four children including Denis, Gerard, and Una. Kernan was educated in the [[Dominicans in Ireland|Dominican College on Eccles St]], because they had a class in physics. She went on to study physics at [[University College Dublin]] graduating with first-class honours in 1952. Kernan was the only woman in the class. After graduation Kernan went on to complete her PhD in physics in her alma mater in 1957. Kernan worked there as a lecturer for four years. She also worked in the University of Rochester.<ref name="The Irish Times 2013">{{cite news | title=Anne Kernan obituary: trailblazing Irish physicist | newspaper=The Irish Times | date=2013-03-21 | url=https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/anne-kernan-obituary-trailblazing-irish-physicist-1.4264877 | access-date=2020-05-30}}</ref><ref name="The Irish Times">{{cite news | title=The Irish 'research lady' who helped win the Nobel | newspaper=The Irish Times | date=2013-03-21 | url=https://www.irishtimes.com/news/science/the-irish-research-lady-who-helped-win-the-nobel-1.637047 | access-date=2020-05-30}}</ref><ref name="JSTOR">{{cite journal | jstor=25504291 | title=University College, Dublin | journal=University Review | year=1954 | volume=1 | issue=3 | pages=93–96 }}</ref><ref name="Panama City News Herald 2020">{{cite web | title=Anne Kernan Obituary - Panama City, FL | website=Panama City News Herald | date=2020-05-15 | url=https://obits.newsherald.com/amp/obituaries/newsherald/196196218 | access-date=2020-05-30 | archive-date=15 July 2020 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200715051119/https://obits.newsherald.com/amp/obituaries/newsherald/196196218 | url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="American Scientist 2017">{{cite web | title=75 Reasons to Become a Scientist | website=American Scientist | date=2017-02-06 | url=https://www.americanscientist.org/article/75-reasons-to-become-a-scientist | access-date=2020-05-30}}</ref><ref name="Department of Physics & Astronomy 2019">{{cite web | title=Graduate Awards | website=Department of Physics & Astronomy | date=2019-09-03 | url=https://physics.ucr.edu/graduate-awards | access-date=2020-05-30}}</ref>

Kernan won a post-doctoral scholarship at the [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory|Lawrence Radiation Laboratory]] at the [[University of California at Berkeley]]. Her next role was at the [[SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory|Stanford Linear Accelerator Center]]. Finally in 1967, she joined the Department of Physics at the [[University of California, Riverside]]. She went on to become chair of the physics department, vice chancellor for research and dean of the graduate division. In each case Kernan was the first woman in all these roles.<ref name="The Irish Times 2013"/><ref name="The Irish Times"/><ref name="Science and National Identity">{{cite web | title=Academic Work in 1950s | website=Science and National Identity | url=http://www.rjtechne.org/century130703/1950s/academ50.htm | access-date=2020-05-30}}</ref><ref name="UCR Profiles">{{cite web | title=Search & Browse | website=UCR Profiles | url=https://profiles.ucr.edu/app/home/profile/annek | access-date=2020-05-30}}</ref><ref name="Department of Physics & Astronomy 2019"/>

==Career==

In 1983, Kernan worked with Professor [[Carlo Rubbia]] and Dr [[Simon van der Meer]]. She led the US team on the [[CERN]] international Nobel-prize winning experiment to discover the two sub-atomic particles, [[W and Z bosons]]. Kernan was invited to the Nobel Prize ceremony in [[Stockholm]]. Kernan was part of the team that went on to discover the [[top quark]] in 1995. She had been working as part of the [[DZero experiment]] at the [[Fermilab|Tevatron collider at the Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory]] near [[Chicago]] since 1986.<ref name="The Irish Times 2013"/><ref name="The Irish Times"/><ref name="Department of Physics & Astronomy 2019"/>

Kernan was a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] and the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]]. She was a supporter of women in [[Science, technology, engineering, and mathematics|STEM]]. She was a member of the American Physics Society committee on the status of women in physics.<ref name="The Irish Times 2013"/><ref name="The Irish Times"/><ref name="Inclusion, Diversity, Equity and Accountability 2014">{{cite web | title=Natalie Roe: How an Early Boost Made a Big Difference | website=Inclusion, Diversity, Equity and Accountability | date=2014-05-19 | url=https://diversity.lbl.gov/2014/05/19/natalie-roe/ | access-date=2020-05-30}}</ref><ref name="Department of Physics & Astronomy 2019"/>

When Kernan retired she moved to Danvers, [[Massachusetts]] to live with her sister and then to [[Panama City Beach]] in [[Florida]] where she died in 2020.<ref name="The Irish Times 2013"/><ref name="The Irish Times"/><ref name="Panama City News Herald 2020"/>
